# #7481: the SHARED corpus for the NAT match-prefix grammar.
#
# One file, read by BOTH the Go gate's test (pkg/config) and the Rust parsers'
# test (userspace-dp/src/nat). Two hand-maintained lists is the disease this
# issue is about, one layer up — the Go predicate claimed by COMMENT to mirror
# the Rust parsers, and it did not.
#
# Format: <verdict> <TAB> <literal>
#   accept  every implementation must accept it
#   reject  every implementation must reject it
#
# A literal is quoted with Go/Rust string syntax so leading and trailing
# whitespace survives the file. Blank lines and #-comments are ignored.
#
# THE GRAMMAR, decided in #7481 rather than inherited:
#   - a CIDR whose prefix length is a decimal within the family's range, with a
#     leading `+` or leading zeros TOLERATED and normalized away
#   - or a bare host address (implicitly /32 or /128)
#   - nothing else: no negative length, no surrounding whitespace, no zone
#     suffix, no second slash
#
# WHY TOLERATE RATHER THAN REJECT. Rejecting the odd spellings is the
# reject-only direction and would normally win. #7145's test says why it does
# not here: a box committed with `match source-address 1.2.3.4/024` is
# forwarding today (static NAT installs it), and a validator widened to refuse a
# working value bricks that operator's next commit (#1960). Both spellings are
# UNAMBIGUOUS — `/+24`, `/024`, `/0024` can only mean 24 — so normalizing loses
# no information and there is no wrong interpretation to pick.
#
# The danger was never the spelling; it was the DISAGREEMENT. Measured, all
# three implementations over this corpus:
#
#   literal            Go ParseCIDR   ipnet::IpNet   u8::from_str
#   10.0.0.0/024       accept         REJECT         accept
#   2001:db8::/064     accept         ACCEPT         accept
#   2001:db8::/0064    accept         reject         accept
#   10.0.0.0/+24       reject         reject         ACCEPT
#
# ipnet disagrees with ITSELF across families on zero padding, so single-
# sourcing the Rust side onto IpNet would still not have produced one grammar.
# `/024` was the worse case: it passed an ordinary strict commit and was then
# DROPPED by parse_match_prefix, leaving a NAT rule that matched nothing.

accept	"10.0.0.0/24"
accept	"10.0.0.5"
accept	"10.0.0.5/24"
accept	"0.0.0.0/0"
accept	"2001:db8::/64"
accept	"2001:db8::1"
accept	"::/0"

# Tolerated spellings — normalized to a plain decimal by every end.
accept	"10.0.0.0/+24"
accept	"10.0.0.0/+0"
accept	"2001:db8::/+64"
accept	"10.0.0.0/024"
accept	"10.0.0.0/0024"
accept	"2001:db8::/064"
accept	"2001:db8::/0064"

# Prefix lengths whose leading zeroes expose the ipnet family asymmetry.
accept	"10.0.0.0/00"
accept	"10.0.0.0/08"
accept	"10.0.0.0/09"
accept	"10.0.0.0/032"
accept	"2001:db8::/0128"
reject	"10.0.0.0/00033"
reject	"2001:db8::/00129"
accept	"10.0.0.0/32"
accept	"2001:db8::1/128"

# A normalized length is still range-checked.
reject	"10.0.0.0/+33"
reject	"10.0.0.0/033"

# Out of range for the family.
reject	"10.0.0.0/33"
reject	"2001:db8::/129"
reject	"10.0.0.0/-1"

# Not an address, or carrying decoration no implementation accepts.
reject	"fe80::1%eth0"
reject	""
reject	" 10.0.0.0/24"
reject	"10.0.0.0/24 "
reject	"10.0.0.0/ 24"
reject	"10.0.0.0/"
reject	"/24"
reject	"not-an-address"
reject	"10.0.0.0/24/24"
